introduction: How did the world begin? The guide gives several answers that it holds together: creation has always been and has no beginning in time, because a Creator must always have a creation; it nevertheless depends at every moment on its cause; the six days of Genesis describe a spiritual order and not a week; things come to be by composition and pass away by dissolution; all was made by a word, out of nothing, and for a purpose, which is knowledge and love of God; and in every age there is a new creation. A hundred of its quotations, a large part of them prayers of praise, are read here with a hundred from elsewhere. Genesis, the psalms, Job, Isaiah, John’s prologue and the Qur’an supply the same praise and many of the same phrases, ‘Be, and it is’ among them. Plato’s craftsman who made the world because he was good, Plotinus’s overflowing One, Aristotle’s unmoved mover, Lao Tzu’s nameless mother of things and the Rig Veda’s hymn that ends in doubt show how others have spoken of beginnings. Heraclitus, Lucretius, Lavoisier and Darwin stand where the guide answers materialism; Genesis’s seventh day stands where it denies that creation ever stopped; and the Preacher asks, twice, whether any of it is new or to any purpose.
questions: The guide says creation has no beginning in time and yet depends wholly on its Creator. How can something be both without beginning and dependent?
It reads the six days of Genesis as a spiritual creation, as Origen did. What is gained and what is risked when a creation story is read in that way?
Lucretius says nothing comes from nothing, and the prayers here praise creation out of nothing. Are they speaking of the same nothing?
Plato says the world was made because its maker was good; the guide says it was made for the knowledge of God. What does each answer ask of a human being?
The Rig Veda ends its hymn by wondering whether even the highest knows how creation arose. What place has that kind of reverent doubt beside the confident praise of these prayers?
The guide speaks of a new creation in each age. What, in your own experience, has it meant for something to be made new?

outside.why: The Rig Veda's hymn of creation asks who knows whence it first came into being, and ends: he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not. What is gained by beginning an account of creation with a confession of that kind?
Plato's Timaeus says that the father and maker of all this universe is past finding out.
Heraclitus says that no one of gods or men has made this world, which was ever and is an ever-living Fire. What separates a world without a maker from a world that has always had one?
Newton says that we know God only by his most wise and excellent contrivances of things, and final causes.
Origen asked who that has understanding will suppose that the first, second and third day existed without a sun, and moon, and stars.
Aristotle's first cause produces motion as being loved, while all other things move by being moved.
Plotinus says that the One, seeking nothing and lacking nothing, has overflowed, and that its exuberance has produced the new.
The Qur'an says that the heavens and the earth were created in six days, and that no weariness touched their maker.
Genesis says that God saw every thing that he had made, and behold, it was very good.
Paul's doxology says the same: of him, and through him, and to him, are all things.
Malachi asks: have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?
Jesus says that the work of God has not stopped: my Father worketh hitherto, and I work.
The Qur'an says that all in the heavens and the earth entreat Him, and that every day He exercises power.
Genesis says that the heavens and the earth were finished, and that God ended his work and rested. How should a finished creation be read beside a creator who has always had a creation?
The psalm says that the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows his handiwork.
Krishna says in the Gita that at the closing of each age all things return to his being, and at its beginning issue forth again.
Paul reasons that the invisible things of God are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood by the things that are made.
Job says: ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee, and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee.
Plato's Timaeus watches the elements pass into one another, water becoming stone and earth by condensation.

Lavoisier found that in every operation an equal quantity of matter exists before and after. If composition and decomposition are all that science observes, where does the question of a composer arise?
Hopkins says that the world is charged with the grandeur of God, and will flame out like shining from shook foil.
Descartes holds that conserving a substance in each moment requires the same power and act as creating it.
The Qur'an speaks of the heaven when it was smoke, and of heaven and earth told to come, willingly or loth.

Darwin finds grandeur in a view of life in which, from so simple a beginning, endless forms have been and are being evolved. Is his account a rival to the divine philosophers' reply, or material for it?
The Preacher watches one generation pass and another come, while the earth abides.
Proverbs says that the Lord by wisdom founded the earth, and by understanding established the heavens.
The psalm says of the making of the world: he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast.
Acts says that God has made of one blood all nations of men to dwell on all the face of the earth.
Tagore says that infinite gifts are poured into very small hands, and still there is room to fill.
Paul speaks of God who quickeneth the dead and calleth those things which be not as though they were.
Lucretius makes it his first principle that nothing from nothing ever yet was born. How does 'creation from nothing' answer the oldest objection to it?
Hebrews says that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things seen were not made of things which do appear.
The Lord asks Job where he was when the foundations of the earth were laid.
The psalm says: before the mountains were brought forth, from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
The Levites' prayer says: thou hast made heaven, the heaven of heavens, the earth and the seas, and thou preservest them all.
Jeremiah says that he has made the earth by his power and established the world by his wisdom.
The name given to Moses at the bush is self-subsistence itself: I AM THAT I AM.
Job says that he stretches out the north over the empty place, and hangs the earth upon nothing.
The psalm says that all creatures wait upon God for their meat in due season.
The psalm says that the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof.
Solomon confesses that the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain God.
The Qur'an says that the heaven and the earth and all between them were not created in play.
The Qur'an invites the eye to look again at the heavens and find no rift.
The Qur'an asks whether there was not a time when man was a thing unremembered.
This phrase is the Qur'an's: His verily is all creation and commandment.
The Qur'an says that as the first creation was begun, so it shall be repeated.
This too is the Qur'an's phrase: He saith unto it, Be! and it is.
Genesis has the same creation by speech: and God said, Let there be light, and there was light.

Lao Tzu speaks of something undefined and complete that came into existence before Heaven and Earth, still and formless, the mother of all things. What changes when the source of the world is one who commands, and what when it is not?
The Qur'an calls him the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward.
John's Gospel says that all things were made by the Word, and without him was not any thing made.
The Qur'an tells its hearers to travel in the land and see how He originated creation.
The psalm says that by the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth.
Paul says that all things were created, in heaven and in earth, visible and invisible.
Isaiah says that God formed the earth and created it not in vain: he formed it to be inhabited.
The psalmist exclaims: O Lord, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all.
The Qur'an finds signs in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day.
Isaiah says: lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things.
Hopkins gives glory to God for dappled things, for skies of couple-colour and whatever is fickle and freckled.
Whitman believes that a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars.
The psalmist considers the heavens, the work of God's fingers, and asks what man is.
Lao Tzu says that all things sprang from It as existing, and that existence sprang from It as non-existent.
Aristotle's God is a thought that thinks only itself. Could such a being will a world, and does the guide's 'absolute Will' answer him?
Augustine says that created things neither altogether are nor altogether are not: they are, because they are from God.
Pope pictures creation as a vast chain of being which from God began.
Dante sees the glory of him who moves everything penetrate the universe, in one part more and in another less.
The Chandogya Upanishad asks how that which is could be born of that which is not. What does 'out of nothing' mean, if it does not mean that?
Hebrews speaks of one by whom the worlds were made, the brightness of God's glory.
Revelation names him Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, which is, and was, and is to come.
The psalm says that the heavens shall wax old like a garment and be changed, but thou art the same.
Lao Tzu counts creation in steps: the Tao produced One, One produced Two, Two produced Three, Three produced all things.
In Proverbs Wisdom says: when he prepared the heavens I was there, and set a compass upon the face of the depth.
Genesis sets lights in the firmament to divide the day from the night, and for signs and seasons.
Emerson says that every natural fact is a symbol of some spiritual fact.
Leibniz says that the connexion of all created things to each makes each simple substance a perpetual living mirror of the universe.
Genesis says that God formed man of the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.
The Qur'an says that man was created from a product of wet earth.
Milton hails holy light, offspring of heaven first-born, bright effluence of bright essence increate.
Genesis says that God made two great lights and set them to give light upon the earth.
Blake would see a world in a grain of sand and hold infinity in the palm of the hand.
Job says that these are parts of his ways, and asks who can understand the thunder of his power.
The psalmist gives thanks: I am fearfully and wonderfully made, marvellous are thy works.
Isaiah prays: we are the clay, and thou our potter, and we all are the work of thy hand.
The Qur'an gives the purpose in one verse: jinn and humankind were created only that they might worship.
Revelation sings that God created all things, and for his pleasure they are and were created.

Plato's Timaeus says that the creator made the world because he was good and without jealousy, and desired all things to be as like himself as they could be. Is that the same reason as 'for the knowledge of God'?
Isaiah hears God say of every one called by his name: I have created him for my glory.
Augustine says that God made us for himself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in him.
The Preacher looked on all the works his hands had wrought and found all vanity, and no profit under the sun. What becomes of a world's purpose when a person cannot find their own?
Jesus says he must work the works of him that sent him while it is day.
Ezekiel is told to call the breath from the four winds to breathe upon the slain, that they may live.
The Preacher says that to every thing there is a season, a time to plant and a time to pluck up.
Paul says that if any man be in Christ he is a new creature: old things are passed away.
Isaiah hears the promise: behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former shall not be remembered.
Revelation hears the one who sat upon the throne say: behold, I make all things new.
The psalm says: thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created, and thou renewest the face of the earth.
The verse continues: the earth was without form and void, and the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.
The Qur'an says that the heavens and the earth were of one piece, and were parted.
The same dialogue begins by asking what always is and has no becoming, and what is always becoming and never is.
The Preacher insists that there is no new thing under the sun. What would he say to a creation that is renewed in every age?

psalm-he-spake-and-it-was-done.text: Let all the earth fear the Lord: let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him. For he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast

psalm-the-earth-is-the-lords.text: The earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. For he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods

proverbs-when-he-prepared-the-heavens.text: When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth: When he established the clouds above: when he strengthened the fountains of the deep: When he gave to the sea his decree, that the waters should not pass his commandment: when he appointed the foundations of the earth: Then I was by him, as one brought up with him: and I was daily his delight, rejoicing always before him; Rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth; and my delights were with the sons of men

isaiah-formed-it-to-be-inhabited.text: For thus saith the Lord that created the heavens; God himself that formed the earth and made it; he hath established it, he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited: I am the Lord; and there is none else

isaiah-created-him-for-my-glory.text: Even every one that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him

revelation-for-thy-pleasure-they-are-cre.text: Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created

jeremiah-made-the-earth-by-his-power.text: He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heavens by his discretion

quran-not-in-play.text: We created not the heaven and the earth and all that is between them in play.

quran-six-days-naught-of-weariness.text: And verily We created the heavens and the earth, and all that is between them, in six Days, and naught of weariness touched Us.

quran-heaven-when-it-was-smoke.text: Then turned He to the heaven when it was smoke, and said unto it and unto the earth: Come both of you, willingly or loth. They said: We come, obedient.

quran-see-how-he-originated-creation.text: See they not how Allah produceth creation, then reproduceth it? Lo! for Allah that is easy. Say (O Muhammad): Travel in the land and see how He originated creation, then Allah bringeth forth the later growth. Lo! Allah is Able to do all things

tao-before-heaven-and-earth.text: There was something undefined and complete, coming into existence before Heaven and Earth. How still it was and formless, standing alone, and undergoing no change, reaching everywhere and in no danger (of being exhausted)! It may be regarded as the Mother of all things
tao-before-heaven-and-earth.author: Laozi

plato-he-was-good.text: Let me tell you then why the creator made this world of generation. He was good, and the good can never have any jealousy of anything. And being free from jealousy, he desired that all things should be as like himself as they could be
plato-he-was-good.author: Plato

rigveda-perhaps-he-knows-not.text: Who knows then whence it first came into being? He, the first origin of this creation, whether he formed it all or did not form it, Whose eye controls this world in highest heaven, he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not
